# Compliance Should Be A Byproduct Of Engineering Practice

## Stance

The controls we assert to an auditor should be the way we already work, recorded by the tools we already use. If a control needs a separate ritual that exists only for the audit, either the control is wrong for us or the practice is missing and we should adopt it for its own sake.

## Scope

Engineering controls: change management, access, incident response, backups, vulnerability management. Less true for HR and vendor controls, where paperwork is part of the practice.

## Why I Think This

- Change management worked because GitHub branch protection records the approval as a side effect of reviewing ([[code-review-policy]]). Nobody fills in a form.
- The access review failed in the Type I because it was a ritual outside any tool or habit ([[soc2-type-1-report]]).
- The incident response control pointed at the runbook we already used ([[run-an-incident]]); the auditor accepted the March postmortem as evidence.

## Where It Gets Uncomfortable

The rule from [[engineering-meeting-2026-04-08]] is a case where the evidence requirement changed the practice: pair-programmed work now also needs a recorded approval. [[hamish-pettigrew]] sees that as compliance overriding engineering judgment, and he has a point. My answer is that a recorded approval is cheap and pairing still happens, but I hold this stance knowing the rule was shaped by the auditor, not by us.

## What Would Change My Mind

If keeping a control "natural" repeatedly leads to exceptions, I would accept more explicit compliance work rather than keep insisting on elegance.
